results.summary: This design implements a hardware inference engine for a simple decision tree, accepting 8-bit feature data and a 2-bit command input while exposing ready, busy, prediction-valid, model-loaded and error status outputs. It produces an 8-bit prediction and supports loading a model through its command interface. The design is controlled through a simple valid/ready handshake with separate command bits. No external hardware is required, and the documentation is limited to the pin names and one-line description.

This design generates a perfect 10x10 maze on-chip using a binary-tree algorithm and displays it over VGA while it is being built. After generation, a player controls a green dot through a PMOD gamepad while a wall-following solver races against them. SELECT regenerates a fresh maze and START accelerates the live build animation. It requires a VGA monitor and a PMOD gamepad as external hardware.

This design counts pulses from four coin sensors representing 10, 5, 2 and 1 baht coins and reports the totals over a UART transmit line. It provides transmit-active, transmit-done and serial-output pins, and takes a switch input alongside the four sensor inputs. Testing involves driving the sensor inputs high and checking that the UART output matches the number of pulses. External hardware includes brightness sensors, buttons and a switch, and the documentation is brief.

This design draws concentric hypnotic squares to a VGA display using the standard Tiny VGA pinout. It is described as an implementation via the VGA playground and can be tested directly in that environment. The only external hardware needed is a VGA PMOD and monitor. The documentation is very thin, consisting of a one-line description and a note about the playground.

This design implements a Pong game rendered over VGA at 25.175 MHz, with two debounced button inputs controlling the paddles. A graphics module compares VGA coordinates against paddle and ball bounds and draws an XOR background, while the ball uses position, velocity and direction registers. It can be tested with the provided Scala test benches or on an FPGA or ASIC connected to a VGA adapter and two buttons. External hardware required is a VGA monitor, cable and two buttons with at least 10k resistors.

This design is a multiply-accumulate unit that operates on 8-bit posit numbers rather than standard floating-point or integer formats. It takes two 8-bit inputs that are successively multiplied and accumulated, with all inputs and outputs exposed on the standard Tiny Tapeout pins. No external hardware is needed to use it. The documentation is minimal, giving only a one-line description and a brief note on how to test it.

This design is an eight-channel 8-bit PWM controller with a UART interface for configuration. Users send eight duty-cycle values between 0 and 254 over UART, which are written to memory, followed by 0xff, 255 to latch them. The eight PWM outputs are exposed on the output pins, and the UART input is on a bidirectional pin. External hardware can include an LED PMOD or a 7-segment PMOD for observing the PWM outputs.

This design implements a small translation lookaside buffer acting as a memory management unit for a TTL logic chip breadboard CPU. It accepts an 8-bit virtual address and produces an 8-bit physical address, with write-enable, read-valid and TLB-hit status signals on the bidirectional pins. The design targets latch-based memory and is intended to sit alongside a discrete CPU. The documentation is very sparse, with no testing instructions or external hardware details provided.

This design renders a large 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo over VGA with bling effects and dithered colors, fitting the whole thing into two tiles. It uses the standard Tiny VGA pinout and is meant to be connected directly to a VGA monitor. The documentation is extremely brief, describing only compressed VGA logo rendering and telling the user to connect a monitor and run it. External hardware required is a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor.

This design is a compact RISC-V RV32I CPU that uses external QSPI PSRAM or flash as its program and data memory, implemented as a state machine for Tiny Tapeout. It includes a 64-bit free-running counter with interrupt, a QSPI memory interface, 4-bit GPIO, 3-bit GPO, 6-bit GPI, one interrupt pin and a UART monitor with commands for memory read/write, breakpoints, register access and execution control. It supports only machine mode, does not implement fence, and ebreak is untested. Testing requires an external QSPI PSRAM and a UART terminal to upload and run programs.
